effect_mechanism: Restored forest recovers biodiversity and vegetation structure relative to degraded land, but not to old-growth levels.
conditionality: Range 15-84% spans moderate to strong on the 10/30% bands; lower end used. Success rises with time since restoration and less fragmented landscapes.
justification: Crouzeilles et al. (2016) Nat. Commun., meta-analysis of 221 landscapes [source_id crouzeilles_2016_restoration_success_meta], PDF p.1: "Our meta-analysis encompassing 221 study landscapes worldwide reveals forest restoration enhances biodiversity by 15–84% and vegetation structure by 36–77%, compared with degraded ecosystems."

effect_mechanism: Restoration raises biodiversity and makes outcomes less variable, but not to reference levels.
conditionality: All terrestrial restoration, not forest only.
justification: Atkinson et al. (2022) Ecol. Lett., meta-analysis of 83 terrestrial restoration studies [source_id atkinson_2022_terrestrial_restoration_biodiv], PDF p.1: "We found that, relative to unrestored (degraded) sites, restoration actions increased biodiversity by an average of 20%, while decreasing the variability of biodiversity (quantified by the coefficient of variation) by an average of 14%."

effect_mechanism: Vegetation cover cuts surface runoff and soil loss.
conditionality: Pools forest and grassland restoration; mostly Chinese studies. SMD -6.23 is strong on the |g|>=0.5 band.
justification: Yang et al. (2023) Soil Tillage Res., meta-analysis of 88 papers [source_id yang_2023_vegrestoration_erosion_meta], PDF p.3: "We found that vegetation restoration could reduce surface runoff (SMD = −2.85; Fig. 2a) and soil loss (SMD = −6.23; Fig. 2b)"

conditionality: Absolute removal rates (9.1-18.8 t CO2/ha/yr for natural regeneration) have no strength band; class is slight by the narrative rule, which almost certainly understates it.
justification: Bernal et al. (2018) Carbon Balance Manag., global review of FLR removal rates [source_id bernal_2018_co2_removal_flr], PDF p.1: "Natural regeneration removal rates were 9.1–18.8 t ­CO2 ­ha−1 ­year−1 during the first 20 years of forest regeneration"

effect_mechanism: Planted trees transpire more, so less water leaves the catchment.
conditionality: Afforestation of grassland and shrubland; eucalypts larger effect; proportionally largest in dry regions.
justification: Farley et al. (2005) Glob. Change Biol., global synthesis of 26 catchment data sets [source_id farley_2005_afforestation_water_yield], PDF p.1: "We found that annual runoff was reduced on average by 44% (  3%) and 31% (  2%) when grasslands and shrublands were afforested, respectively."

effect_mechanism: Most studies find water yield falls after forest restoration or expansion.
conditionality: Narrative direction only (slight by rule); few studies of native-species restoration or of large/long projects; humid tropics under-studied.
justification: Filoso et al. (2017) PLOS ONE, systematic review [source_id filoso_2017_restoration_water_yield_sr], PDF p.1: "Most studies reported decreases in water yields following the intervention, while other hydrological benefits have been observed."

effect_mechanism: Peak flow falls by about half the forest-cover change.
justification: Herath et al. (2025) J. Flood Risk Manag., systematic review of 50 catchment studies [source_id herath_2025_forest_cover_flood_sr], PDF p.1: "Forest cover consistently impacts peak flow across catchments of all sizes, with a generalized linear rela- tionship where the effect magnitude is approximately half the forest cover change. For example, a 20% increase in forest cover tends to reduce peak flow by 10% across small, medium, and large catchments."

effect_mechanism: Benefit for small rainfall events only; limited for major floods.
justification: FAO & CIFOR (2005) Forests and floods, RAP 2005/03 [source_id fao_cifor_2005_forests_floods], PDF p.13: "Contrary to popular belief, forests have only a limited inﬂ uence on major downstream ﬂ ooding, especially large-scale events."

effect_mechanism: Dry-season flow sustained in treated catchments.
conditionality: Bundled with soil and water conservation works; Ethiopia only.
justification: Meaza et al. (2022) Land Degrad. Dev., meta-analysis of 361 paired catchments (Ethiopia) [source_id meaza_2022_catchment_restoration_drought_meta], PDF p.1: "Such consistent water flow reduced hydrological, agricultural and socioeconomic drought effects in treated catchment."

effect_mechanism: Forest gain cools the land surface.
conditionality: Land surface temperature, not human heat stress.
justification: Prevedello et al. (2019) PLOS ONE, global remote-sensing analysis [source_id prevedello_2019_forestation_local_temperature], PDF p.1: "Deforestation from 2000 to 2010 caused consistent warming of 0.38 ± 0.02 (mean ± SE) and 0.16 ± 0.01˚C in tropical and temperate regions respectively, while forestation caused cooling in those regions of -0.18 ± 0.02 and -0.19 ± 0.02˚C. Tropical forests were particularly sensitive to the climate effects of forest change, with forest cover losses of ~50% associated with increased LST of 1.08 ± 0.25˚C, whereas similar forest cover gains decreased LST by -1.11"

effect_mechanism: Short-term income from paid tree planting; little evidence that services from the restored forest reduce poverty.
conditionality: Assessment notes multiple case studies but few with robust counterfactuals (confidence low as stated).
justification: Miller, Mansourian & Wildburger (eds.) (2020) IUFRO GFEP Forests, Trees and the Eradication of Poverty, ch. 5 [source_id iufro_2020_gfep_forests_poverty], PDF p.132: "Evidence shows that forest restoration, reforestation or afforestation can result in short-term livelihood benefits from direct involvement in tree planting (e.g. via payments and increased asset ownership). There is little evidence that livelihood benefits from services provided by restored forests meaningfully benefit proximate households to alleviate poverty."
